opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at first I didn't really know what research *was*. I just knew I liked building things and figuring out why they worked, and I had this vague sense that the people pushing the frontier were in labs, not just in classrooms.

So the first thing I did was pretty unglamorous: I started reading. I'd go through faculty pages in the computer science department, look at their projects, and try to read their papers. Most of it went over my head at first, but I'd pick out the ones that excited me, especially anything involving robots or getting machines to perceive and interact with the world.

Then I just started emailing professors. A lot of those emails went unanswered, which is normal, and I think every undergrad should expect that. But I tried to make each email specific. I'd say what I'd read, what I found interesting, and what skills I could actually bring, even if that was just "I can write code and I'm willing to do the boring stuff."

Eventually a lab let me in, and that's where the real learning started. As a first- or second-year you're not designing the big ideas. You're setting up hardware, debugging code, running experiments that fail for reasons nobody understands. But being around grad students and seeing how they thought about problems taught me more than any course. I learned that research is mostly persistence, asking good questions, and being okay with being confused for a long time.

Looking back, my advice would be: don't wait until you feel "ready." Nobody feels ready. Show genuine curiosity, be specific about why you want to join, and once you're in, be the person who's reliable and keeps showing up. That opened every door after that for me.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it started pretty clumsily. I came into college knowing I wanted to do research, but I had no idea what that actually meant day to day. So the first thing I did was just read a lot — I'd go through papers in areas I thought were interesting, mostly robotics and perception at the time, and I'd understand maybe a third of what was on the page. But that reading gave me enough vocabulary to send emails to professors that didn't sound completely clueless.

And I sent a lot of emails. Most of them went unanswered, which I now understand is totally normal, but at the time it felt pretty discouraging. Eventually one lab took me on, and my first job was basically data collection and cleaning up code that a grad student had written. It was not glamorous. But I think that was actually the most important part — being in the room, going to group meetings, hearing how people argued about what to try next. You learn what a research question even looks like by watching people fail to answer one for a few months.

The other thing I did, which I'd recommend to anyone, was to take on little side projects on my own. Not for a class, not for credit, just things I was curious about. Can I get this robot simulator to do X? Can I reproduce this result from a paper? Half of them didn't work. But reproducing things taught me more about how papers are actually made than any lecture did, and it gave me something concrete to show when I asked for more responsibility in the lab.

So I'd say the pattern was: read enough to be dangerous, be persistent about getting a foot in the door, accept the unglamorous work, and keep building things on the side so you have your own momentum rather than waiting for someone to hand you a problem.
